title: What If the Sea Froze Solid? In 1658 an Army Marched Across It and Won a War

scenes.text: What if the sea froze hard enough to march an army across? In 1658 one did.
The 1600s were the coldest century of the Little Ice Age. Scandinavian winters were brutal.
In January 1658 the straits between Denmark's islands froze. Sweden's King Charles the Tenth saw a road.
On 30 January his army crossed the Little Belt on the ice, engineers testing it ahead. Then the Great Belt, island to island.
The ice cracked under the king's hunting sled after he had left it. Two cavalry squadrons broke through and drowned.
By 15 February the Swedes stood near Copenhagen. On 26 February Denmark signed the Treaty of Roskilde and gave up Scania for good.

description:
What if the sea froze hard enough to march an army across? In the winter of 1658, during the coldest century of the Little Ice Age, King Charles X Gustav of Sweden led his army over the frozen Little Belt and Great Belt, island by island, towards Copenhagen.
Two cavalry squadrons drowned when the ice gave way, but by 15 February the Swedes were outside the capital, and on 26 February 1658 Denmark signed the Treaty of Roskilde, ceding Scania, Halland and Blekinge, which remain Swedish today.
